newsitem.title: UK: Natural rubber market seen in deficit by 1998.
newsitem.headline: Natural rubber market seen in deficit by 1998.

text.p: The world's natural rubber market is heading for a supply deficit of 80,000 tonnes in calendar 1998, against expected surpluses of 10,000 tonnes in 1996 and 20,000 in 1997, the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) said.
Fundamentals suggested the market was again moving towards a shortage, although this would be as severe as in 1994, the EIU said in the latest edition of its World Commodity Profiles.

"We expect this to be reflected in an increasingly firm market," it said, putting prices of the key RSS1 rubber grade at 1,260 stg a tonne in 1998, up from an estimated 990 stg in 1996 and 1,170 in 1997.
On the supply side, the EIU said growth potential seemed limited. Growing supplies from China and Vietnam could be offset by lower output from Malaysia, Sri Lanka and the Philippines.
Higher prices in 1994 and 1995 had revived investment interest in rubber planting in Brazil, but it took at least four years for trees to become tappable.
It said the future of the new International Natural Rubber Agreement (INRA), a producer-consumer price-stabilisation pact, now seemed assured with the belated accession of the U.S.
INRA's buffer stock operation was expected to have a calming influence on prices in the long term.
